triage.name: Campylobacter Infections
triage.reason: Acute diarrheal illness with food/exposure history; students work through the infectious diarrhea differential and stool testing.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'stool culture' was in ['initial', 'confirmatory'], kept ['initial']

demographics: One of the most common causes of bacterial diarrhea worldwide
Sporadic cases rather than large outbreaks are typical
More common in children under 5 and in young adults

risk_factors.text: Handling raw poultry or infected animal feces without handwashing
Contact with puppies or kittens with diarrhea
Travel to areas with poor sanitation
Men who have sex with men

social_history: Food preparation at home involving raw poultry
Occupational or recreational animal contact (farm, pet store, veterinary work)

chief_complaints.text: I've had watery diarrhea for a few days
I feel feverish and wiped out

hpi.onset: Gradual, starting 2–5 days after the contaminated meal or exposure
hpi.duration: Usually about one week; diarrhea can linger up to 2 weeks
hpi.progression: Begins with fever, headache and muscle aches, then crampy abdominal pain followed by diarrhea that may become bloody; symptoms peak over 1–3 days and then slowly improve
hpi.location: Diffuse abdominal cramping, often periumbilical or lower abdomen
hpi.quality: Crampy, colicky abdominal pain with frequent loose stools
hpi.severity: Moderate; cramps come in waves and are uncomfortable but usually tolerable
hpi.timing: Cramps come and go and often precede each bowel movement
pertinent_negatives: Vomiting that started before the diarrhea
Bloody diarrhea with no fever or cramps
Weight loss over weeks to months

argues_against: Migratory joint pain weeks after the diarrhea
Ascending symmetric weakness weeks after the diarrhea

atypical.how_it_differs: Diarrhea can be prolonged, relapsing or severe, and bacteremia with systemic illness occurs; symptoms may last weeks and require antibiotics.
Infants and young children present with irritability, poor feeding and dehydration rather than describing cramps; bloody stools are more common.
May present with dehydration, confusion or generalized weakness rather than prominent diarrhea, and illness can be more severe.

general.mild: Alert, well-appearing, comfortable between cramps; no dehydration
general.moderate: Uncomfortable, flushed, mild dehydration (dry mucous membranes, slightly reduced skin turgor)
general.severe: Ill-appearing, restless or lethargic, moderate dehydration (sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill, tachycardia)
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic, severe dehydration or shock (hypotension, mottled skin, minimal urine output)

findings.finding: Diffuse or periumbilical tenderness without focal guarding or rebound

findings.maneuver: Auscultate bowel sounds in all quadrants
Palpate deeply and ask the patient to cough
findings.finding: No involuntary guarding, rigidity or rebound tenderness

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue
Pinch the skin over the forearm or abdomen
findings.finding: Reduced skin turgor with slow recoil

findings.maneuver: Press the fingertip and time capillary refill
Inspect and palpate the knees, ankles and wrists
findings.finding: No joint swelling, warmth or effusion

findings.maneuver: Test lower extremity strength, deep tendon reflexes and sensation

labs.caveat: A normal white count does not rule out Campylobacter; leukocytosis with a left shift is more typical of invasive, bloody diarrhea.
Falls only with heavy or prolonged bloody diarrhea; anemia is not typical of uncomplicated disease.
Hyponatremia from gastrointestinal losses and replacement with free water.
Hypokalemia from diarrheal losses; can be marked in severe or prolonged diarrhea.
Low bicarbonate reflects a non-gap metabolic acidosis from stool bicarbonate losses.
Prerenal elevation from dehydration and poor intake; falls with rehydration.
Acute kidney injury from hypovolemia; usually improves with fluids.
May be only mildly elevated; a low value does not exclude bacterial enteritis.
Elevated only with hypoperfusion from severe dehydration or sepsis.
Can be positive from dehydration or hematuria in hemolytic uremic syndrome; not a routine test for diarrhea.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia from fever and dehydration
Sinus rhythm; no arrhythmia expected from the infection itself
Nonspecific ST-T flattening with hypokalemia from diarrheal losses

findings.text: Nonspecific bowel gas pattern; no obstruction or free air
Dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels suggesting ileus
Free intraperitoneal air (perforation) — not expected in Campylobacter enteritis

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Severe pain, suspected colitis, toxic megacolon, abscess or perforation

findings.text: Diffuse colonic wall thickening with mucosal enhancement
Free air or abscess indicating perforation

imaging.preferred_when: Children or pregnancy when another diagnosis such as appendicitis or intussusception is considered

imaging.study: MRI abdomen and pelvis without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Pregnancy when CT is needed but radiation should be avoided

findings.text: Colonic wall thickening and pericolonic edema

initial.why: Leukocytosis with a left shift supports bacterial enteritis; anemia suggests heavy blood loss
Assesses dehydration, electrolyte losses and acute kidney injury
Identifies Campylobacter and guides antibiotic choice in moderate to severe or bloody diarrhea
Supports an inflammatory bacterial cause when culture is not immediately available
Rules out pregnancy before antibiotics or imaging in anyone who could be pregnant

confirmatory.test: Campylobacter stool PCR (multiplex GI pathogen panel)
confirmatory.why: Rapid and sensitive molecular detection when available; may not report susceptibility

supporting.why: Supports an inflammatory process but is nonspecific
May help distinguish bacterial from viral diarrhea, though it is often only mildly elevated
Detects bacteremia in severe or immunocompromised patients
supporting.only_if: severe illness, high fever, or immunocompromised

supporting.why: Evaluates for parasitic causes when diarrhea is prolonged or travel-related
supporting.only_if: prolonged diarrhea, travel history, or exposure to untreated water

not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management in uncomplicated diarrhea
not_indicated.only_if: suspected obstruction, toxic megacolon or perforation

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not needed for typical self-limited enteritis
not_indicated.only_if: severe pain, suspected colitis, abscess or perforation

not_indicated.why: No role unless the pain is epigastric or pancreatitis is suspected
No role in the evaluation of diarrhea
Not part of the acute workup; consider only for chronic diarrhea

decision_points: Stool culture is most useful in bloody, severe, prolonged or immunocompromised cases; most mild cases need no testing
Pregnancy test before antibiotics or imaging in anyone who could be pregnant
Bloody diarrhea with fever and cramps suggests an invasive bacterial cause and warrants stool testing
Persistent diarrhea beyond 2 weeks should prompt evaluation for parasites or other chronic causes

differential.name: Salmonella gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Acute inflammatory diarrhea with fever and cramps after a foodborne exposure
differential.trigger: Bloody diarrhea with fever after eating undercooked poultry or eggs, or after contact with reptiles or chicks

history: Exposure to eggs, poultry, reptiles or chicks
Symptoms often begin 6–48 hours after exposure
exam: Rose spots or splenomegaly suggest enteric fever rather than simple gastroenteritis
imaging: Usually normal; CT may show ileocolitis

differential.name: Shigella infection
differential.why_considered: Bloody diarrhea with fever, cramps and tenesmus
differential.trigger: Very low-volume bloody stools with severe tenesmus and fever

history: Person-to-person spread in daycare or crowded settings
imaging: Not routinely needed; CT may show colitis

differential.name: Escherichia coli O157:H7 infection
differential.why_considered: Bloody diarrhea after eating undercooked ground beef or contaminated produce
differential.trigger: Bloody diarrhea without high fever, especially after ground beef, with pallor or decreasing urine output

history: Exposure to undercooked ground beef, unpasteurized milk or contaminated produce
Bloody diarrhea with minimal or no fever
May progress to hemolytic uremic syndrome
exam: Pallor, petechiae or edema suggest hemolytic uremic syndrome
labs: Stool culture on sorbitol-MacConkey agar or Shiga toxin testing
Anemia, thrombocytopenia and elevated creatinine suggest hemolytic uremic syndrome

differential.name: Viral gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Acute watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting and cramps

labs: Stool studies negative for bacterial pathogens

differential.name: Clostridioides difficile colitis
differential.why_considered: Diarrhea with abdominal pain and fever, sometimes bloody
differential.trigger: Recent antibiotic use, hospitalization or long-term care stay

history: Recent antibiotic use within the past 2 months
labs: Stool C. difficile toxin or PCR positive
imaging: CT may show colonic wall thickening and pericolonic stranding

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis)
differential.why_considered: Chronic or recurrent diarrhea with abdominal pain, sometimes bloody

history: Extraintestinal symptoms such as joint pain or rash
exam: Perianal fistulas or skin tags in Crohn disease
labs: Stool studies negative for acute bacterial pathogens
imaging: Colonic or terminal ileal wall thickening on CT or MRI

differential.name: Yersinia enterocolitica infection
differential.why_considered: Diarrhea with abdominal pain that can mimic appendicitis

history: Exposure to undercooked pork or contaminated milk
exam: May have erythema nodosum or reactive arthritis
imaging: CT may show terminal ileitis and mesenteric lymphadenopathy

differential.name: Giardiasis
differential.why_considered: Prolonged watery diarrhea and bloating after travel or untreated water exposure

history: Prolonged diarrhea with bloating and foul-smelling stools
Travel to areas with poor sanitation or drinking untreated water
labs: Stool ova and parasites positive for Giardia

severity.mild: Watery diarrhea without blood, mild cramps, low-grade or no fever, no dehydration; self-limited over about a week
severity.moderate: Frequent diarrhea, sometimes bloody, with fever, significant cramps and mild dehydration; may require antibiotics
severity.severe: Bloody diarrhea, high fever, severe abdominal pain, moderate dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities or acute kidney injury; requires antibiotics and possibly hospitalization
severity.critical: Bacteremia with sepsis, toxic megacolon, perforation or severe dehydration with shock; life-threatening

red_flags.meaning: Invasive bacterial infection; warrants stool testing and consideration of antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Signs of severe dehydration (sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill, hypotension, minimal urine output)
red_flags.meaning: Requires immediate fluid resuscitation and possible hospitalization

red_flags.finding: Severe abdominal pain with distension and absent bowel sounds
red_flags.meaning: Possible toxic megacolon or ileus; urgent imaging and surgical consultation

red_flags.finding: Immunocompromised state with prolonged or severe diarrhea
red_flags.meaning: Higher risk of bacteremia and prolonged illness; lower threshold for antibiotics and blood cultures

red_flags.finding: Neurologic symptoms weeks after diarrhea (weakness, tingling, difficulty walking)
red_flags.meaning: Possible Guillain-Barré syndrome; urgent neurologic evaluation

complications.name: Reactive arthritis
clues: Joint pain and swelling weeks after diarrhea

special_populations.differences: Infants and young children present with irritability, poor feeding and dehydration rather than describing cramps; bloody stools are more common. Fluid management is critical.
May present with dehydration, confusion or generalized weakness rather than prominent diarrhea; illness can be more severe and complications more likely.
Diarrhea can be prolonged, relapsing or severe, and bacteremia with systemic illness occurs; symptoms may last weeks and require antibiotics.
Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance can affect both mother and fetus; antibiotics should be chosen with fetal safety in mind, and fluid resuscitation is important.

key_questions.question: When did the diarrhea start, and how has it changed since then?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset 2–5 days after a contaminated meal or exposure; watery diarrhea that may become bloody, peaking over 1–3 days then slowly improving

key_questions.question: Is there blood or mucus in your stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Bloody or mucoid stools suggest an invasive bacterial cause such as Campylobacter and warrant stool testing

key_questions.question: How many stools a day, and how would you describe them?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequent loose or watery stools; small-volume bloody stools with tenesmus point more toward Shigella

key_questions.question: What have you eaten in the past week — especially chicken, turkey, or other poultry?
key_questions.looking_for: Undercooked or raw poultry, the strongest exposure for Campylobacter

key_questions.question: Have you had unpasteurized milk or cheese, or untreated water from a well or stream?
key_questions.looking_for: Raw milk or untreated water exposure, both classic Campylobacter sources

key_questions.question: Have you been around puppies, kittens, or farm animals with diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact with young pets or livestock, a recognized source of Campylobacter

key_questions.question: Have you taken antibiotics in the past 2 months, or been in a hospital or long-term care facility?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent antibiotics or hospitalization raises concern for C. difficile colitis rather than Campylobacter

key_questions.question: Do you have a condition or take a medication that weakens your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: HIV, transplant, or immunosuppressive therapy — higher risk of prolonged illness and bacteremia, lowering the threshold for antibiotics and blood cultures

key_questions.question: Any fever, chills, or feeling wiped out?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever and fatigue are common; high fever with chills raises concern for bacteremia

key_questions.question: Any nausea or vomiting, and did the vomiting start before or after the diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting after the diarrhea fits Campylobacter; vomiting first suggests viral gastroenteritis

key_questions.question: How much are you drinking, and how often are you urinating?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor intake or reduced urine output signals dehydration and need for fluids

key_questions.question: Have you noticed weakness, tingling, or trouble walking?
key_questions.looking_for: Ascending symmetric weakness or tingling weeks after diarrhea suggests Guillain-Barré syndrome and needs urgent neurologic evaluation

reasoning_points: Acute diarrheal illness beginning 2–5 days after a contaminated food or water exposure
Exposure to undercooked poultry, unpasteurized milk, untreated water, or young pets with diarrhea
Crampy abdominal pain with fever and watery diarrhea that may become bloody
Diffuse or periumbilical abdominal tenderness without focal peritoneal signs
Leukocytosis with a left shift supporting an invasive bacterial cause
Stool culture or multiplex GI pathogen PCR identifies Campylobacter
Pregnancy excluded before antibiotics or imaging when relevant
Alternative causes such as C. difficile, Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli O157:H7, and viral gastroenteritis considered and addressed

easy: Young adult with classic watery then bloody diarrhea 3 days after undercooked chicken
Crampy periumbilical pain with fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness
Leukocytosis with a left shift and a positive stool culture for Campylobacter
medium: Patient with bloody diarrhea and fever where Shigella or Salmonella must be distinguished
Recent antibiotic use raising concern for C. difficile colitis
Mild watery diarrhea without blood where viral gastroenteritis is the main alternative
Dehydration with electrolyte abnormalities and acute kidney injury
hard: Immunocompromised patient with prolonged or relapsing diarrhea and possible bacteremia
Older adult presenting with confusion or generalized weakness rather than prominent diarrhea
Child with irritability, poor feeding, and bloody stools where intussusception or appendicitis is considered
Diarrhea followed weeks later by reactive arthritis or ascending weakness suggesting Guillain-Barré syndrome
